cards.title: Liz Kowalczyk
cards.prompt: One reporter and the ECRI Institute went through the FDA's adverse-event database for deaths involving monitor alarms, and found the Boston death was one of hundreds. Who was she, for which paper, and how many manufacturer reports did that review cover?
cards.answer: Liz Kowalczyk of the Boston Globe. She and ECRI reviewed 216 reports manufacturers had filed with the FDA on deaths in which monitor alarm problems occurred, covering 2005 to the middle of 2010.
cards.body: The Globe enlisted ECRI, a non-profit health care research group, to help it work through the FDA's database of adverse events involving medical devices: 216 manufacturer reports on deaths where monitor alarms were involved, 2005 to the middle of 2010. Her February 2011 series also logged a 15-bed unit averaging 942 alarms a day.

cards.title: The morning ten nurses heard nothing
cards.prompt: Lower-level alarms warned of his falling heart rate — at the central station, across three hallway signs — and nobody came. How many nurses were on duty, what reason did the unit's staff give investigators, and what did the family settle for?
cards.answer: Ten nurses, none of whom could recall the beeps or the scrolling signs. Nursing staff interviewed on the patient care unit told state investigators they were experiencing alarm fatigue and a desensitization to alarms after hearing them constantly throughout the workday. The family settled for $850,000. The crisis alarm that would have cut through had been switched off, and investigators never said why.
cards.body: An 89-year-old man's heart rate fell over 20 minutes and stopped. The lower-level alarms fired — at the nurses' station, across three hallway signs — and none of them landed; the crisis alarm was off. What had run out was not the channel but the receiver: the signals arrived and nobody registered them.

cards.title: Sentinel Event Alert, Issue 50
cards.prompt: Three years later the body that accredits US hospitals published its own count of alarm-related deaths. Name the document and its date, and give its two headline ratios: how many alarm signals a patient generates per day, and what share of them need no clinical action.
cards.answer: Sentinel Event Alert, Issue 50, 'Medical device alarm safety in hospitals', 8 April 2013. Alarm signals can reach several hundred per patient per day; an estimated 85 to 99 percent require no clinical intervention.
cards.body: Its own Sentinel Event database held 98 alarm-related events between January 2009 and June 2012: 80 deaths, 13 permanent losses of function, five extended stays. The largest single reported contributing factor was alarm signals inappropriately turned off, at 36. Alarm fatigue, the alert says, is the most common one.

cards.title: Why priority has to be physical
cards.sub: 2013 · from the ward to your queue
cards.prompt: If 85 to 99 percent of a ward's alarms need no action, why does turning the crisis alarm up fail to fix anything, and what does that force you to do with the priority field on a notification?
cards.answer: Because the saturated resource is the receiver, not the channel: volume cannot buy back attention the bulk traffic already spent. So priority stops being a field and becomes physical separation — its own lane, workers and provider budget per class — and the bulk rate cap stops being courtesy and becomes P0-availability insurance.
cards.body: Volume is one line of the alert: check that critical alarm signals are audible. The recommendations that change the load are different - an inventory of alarm-equipped devices, default settings per care area, guidelines for tailoring limits to each patient, and written identification of when an alarm signal is not clinically necessary. Priority made physical, class by class.
